name: Forensics CLI 101: The Aurora Case
description: A digital-forensics case worked from the command line, from arriving at the bench to carving a file out of a disk image. Written for a cyber-forensics course, and it teaches general CLI skill through the case. Assumes you have met a terminal before.
// scene: The wide establishing shot across the top of the briefing: the place the story opens. Optional. Same image rules as cover -- raster only, never SVG, never a web address. Pairs with reveal, which is the same place once the story has ended.
// reveal: The picture the class uncovers together, one square per find. Embedded, so a pack stays one file. Raster only -- never SVG.
// revealCaption: The line printed under the picture when the last square turns over. It names what the class uncovered, so the picture is the end of the scenario rather than decoration. It must never contain an answer -- a class finishes the picture before its slowest student finishes the pack.
revealCaption: The container is open. This is what left Aurora Robotics at 02:18 on the fifteenth of March — the prototype drawings, all 412 files of them. The case is closed.
// glossary: What this course's own vocabulary means. The engine defines the shell -- what `grep` is, what a pipe does -- because that never varies by course. These are forensics terms and this pack's own commands, which no engine table could know. A key here overrides the engine's for this pack only.

magic-bytes.what: The first few bytes of a file, which say what it really is. A file's extension is a claim; its magic bytes are the evidence.

binary-analysis.what: A file that is not text. You cannot read it directly, but readable fragments are usually still inside it.

chain-of-custody.what: The unbroken record of who held an exhibit and what they did to it. A finding nobody can trace back is a finding that will not stand.

evidence-carving.what: Cutting a file out of a larger image by its position, rather than by asking a filesystem for it. It is how you recover something the filesystem no longer lists.

mmls.what: `mmls` prints a disk image's partition table: which sector each partition starts at, how long it is, and what kind it is. It reads the image and changes nothing in it.

partition-tables.what: The map at the start of a disk saying where each partition begins and ends. Read it and you know where to cut.

sector-offsets.what: How far into a disk something starts, counted in sectors rather than bytes. Carry the number exactly; a tool will refuse a wrong one.

multi-step-forensics.what: Taking a number out of one tool's output and into the next tool's argument. Most real forensic work is this, done carefully.

wsl-paths.what: Windows Subsystem for Linux: a Linux shell running on a Windows machine, able to see both filesystems at once.

/mnt/c.what: Where WSL mounts the Windows C: drive. `C:\Users` appears as `/mnt/c/Users`, reachable with ordinary Linux commands.

path-translation.what: The same file has two names on a machine running both systems: `C:\Users\x` to Windows and `/mnt/c/Users/x` to Linux.

briefing.heading: The Aurora Case
briefing.body:
You are first on scene at the bench. The exhibits are logged, the machine is yours, and the case will be built from what you can show — not from what you remember doing.

Forensics work is ordinary command-line work done carefully. You will look at files without changing them, prove what a file really is rather than what it claims to be, and carry a number from one command into the next without writing it down wrong.

Act VI moves to the seized Windows laptop and does the same work again in cmd.exe, because a case does not choose its operating system for you.
youWillLearn: Get your bearings on an unfamiliar machine
Read a file’s true type from its magic bytes, not its extension
Take and check a forensic hash
Search a filesystem with grep and find
Build multi-stage pipelines that answer a real question
Read a partition table and carry a sector offset
Do the same work again in Windows CMD

messages.unsimulated: That is a real command, but not simulated in this lab. Type `help` to see what works here.
messages.unsupportedSyntax: That shell syntax is not simulated here.

courseTools.hexdump: a hex viewer used to inspect file headers
courseTools.xxd: a hex viewer used to inspect file headers
courseTools.sha1sum: a hashing tool (this simulator has md5sum and sha256sum)
courseTools.openssl: a crypto toolkit used for hashing and certificates
courseTools.fsstat: a Sleuth Kit tool for filesystem details
courseTools.fls: a Sleuth Kit tool for listing files, including deleted ones
courseTools.icat: a Sleuth Kit tool for extracting file content by inode
courseTools.mactime: a Sleuth Kit tool for building timelines
courseTools.exiftool: a metadata reader for documents and images
courseTools.vol: the Volatility 3 command for memory forensics
courseTools.autopsy: the graphical front end to the Sleuth Kit

acts.name: Act I: First on Scene
acts.tagline: Get your bearings on the bench: paths, prompt, and what is really in a directory

acts.name: Act II: Reading the Evidence
acts.tagline: Open the exhibits: file contents, true file types, and forensic checksums

acts.name: Act III: Following the Trail
acts.tagline: Search, find, manual pages, and the WSL bridge to the seized laptop

acts.name: Act IV: The Pipeline
acts.tagline: Pipes, redirection, filters, and multi-stage analysis

acts.name: Act V: Closing the Case
acts.tagline: Read the partition table, carry the offset, carve the container

acts.name: Act VI: The Seized Laptop (Windows)
acts.tagline: Windows CMD parity: dir /a, type, findstr, attrib, and certutil
